title: If AI writes the retrospective, does anyone learn?
summary: Writing a retro is a small part of the learning process. One incident told three ways shows what AI can take on, and what still takes people talking to people.
body_markdown:
AI can make it easy to establish facts during an incident, like the order of events and names of people and services involved. Think of this like the plot. Romeo and Juliet first meet in Act 1, Scene 5 at Lord Capulet’s mansion. These are all relevant facts to the story. The facts don’t carry any of the significance of Shakespeare’s prose.


> So what is the point of a retrospective? Is it a record of facts, or is it an instrument to affect how people think?


## Report, analysis, or investigation?


Here’s a paraphrasing of an incident report taken recently from a hyperscaler. Details left out for anonymity, but the incident itself is fairly typical.


This particular hyperscaler provided IaaS for an extremely high traffic social media application. One day, alarms started going off because the capacity footprint for the social media application was not growing with diurnal patterns in utilization. The infrastructure was expected to autoscale up and down twice daily, and it wasn’t scaling up. It was noticed that the control plane responsible for autoscaling data was not functioning. It was then noticed that the control plane was down because a critical database had been deleted in the production environment. The human who deleted the database was identified, some people jumped in to assist restoration of the database from a backup, and everything came back online to normal operating parameters. In total, the incident lasted a few hours and customer impact was minimal: increased error rates and slower response rates.


## The report


At this particular organization, they followed a typical “root cause analysis” (RCA) process embellished with “correction of error” (COE)-style action items for follow up. The RCA/COE went something like this:


Deletion of the database was the root cause of the incident. No one should be able to manually delete a database in production. Some senior technical people went so far as to suggest that this displayed unacceptably poor judgment and was therefore a fire-able offense. Choice quote: “Even a junior dev out of college knows not to delete a database in production.” To make sure that this never happens again, guardrails would be put in place to prevent database deletion, and processes like two-person rules would be enacted for all critical database operations for the control plane.


I’d call this an incident *report* . A group of people who were involved are looking back on the incident, with the facts that they have at hand, and documenting a narrative supported by those facts plus their personal experience and the culture of the org.


Three things jump out at me from this report:


1. The root cause is coincidentally also the thing mitigated to bring the system back online. That’s always suspicious, but it’s also common and expedient in retrospectives.
2. Guardrails are suggested as an action item. That deserves another blog post, but generally speaking guardrails, like all defense-in-depth or swiss cheese approaches, are ineffective as a preventative measure in complex systems.
3. The voice of the person who deleted the database is noticeably absent.


### Could AI help with the report? Yes, absolutely!


The report by its nature generalizes over the common experience of technical participants within the framework (RCA/COE) enforced by the organization. There is an implied template to this report, and AI can fill in the missing values to summarize the order of events. Similarly, the action items follow a pattern. All of this can be generated from observability tooling and Slack transcripts. Heck, the experienced technical people don’t even need to be brought in to pontificate. They can simply be sent the report automatically.


### Is this report useful? No, probably not.


If we squint, we can say that we learned that databases in production can be manually deleted, and that might be news to the team. Otherwise, what did we learn? Not much at all. This activity primarily served the purpose of checking a box for the larger organization. An incident happened, and this is proof that some people[paid attention](https://rootly.com/blog/human-in-the-loop-is-the-new-pay-attention) to it.


## The analysis


In this case, because of the three things that jumped out about the report, we decided to spend a little more time looking into the incident. We looked at metrics for surrounding services and team logs, and found some additional facts that we consider interesting and relevant:


- The team that deleted the database already has a two-person rule in place.
- It was documented that the person who deleted the database had consulted with the rest of the team, and all members agreed to the action.
- The deletion was initiated to satisfy other operational concerns.
- At the time of deletion, that database had an abnormally low number of concurrent connections, signifying low utilization.
- The timing of the deletion was coincident with the upswing in the diurnal traffic pattern, most likely because it took place during business hours for the operations team.


Based on this information, the action items in the COE are moot. We now have a better picture of what happened, and how it happened, based on the information available.


I’d call this an incident *analysis* . We took a broader look at correlated data and created a richer narrative that focuses more on understanding what was happening at the time, and focused less on what could be done to prevent similar incidents in the future.


### Could AI help with the analysis? Probably.


It might take more tokens to ‘think’ harder about the incident and examine additional data sources. A well-tuned AI agent could identify additional paths in the code and in operational practices that end up in the undesired result. It certainly feels like casting a wider net can generate more context about what happened, and that changes how we think about the incident.


### Is the analysis useful? Maybe.


At the very least, we know now that the COE format didn’t produce useful action items. If action items are required, we need to come up with something else to check that box. Ideally, the outcome of the analysis is *learning* . When[learning is the desired outcome](https://www.adaptivecapacitylabs.com/2025/02/28/what-progress-in-learning-from-incidents-actually-looks-like/) , the point of the exercise isn’t to generate action items, but to create a narrative that reaches the broadest audience. We want to teach as many people as we can about properties of the system that they didn’t know before.


## The investigation


We now have some context about the team that deleted the database, but we still haven’t captured the voice of the person who did it. So, we decided to spend a little more time and dig a little bit deeper.


We interviewed several people involved in the incident including the person who deleted the database, and tried to understand: Why did it make sense to you at the time, to delete this database in production? Again paraphrasing, here’s what we found:


The database in question was co-located with several others on a logical volume with hard storage limits. The team was working through tickets assigned to them by a Security team. Specifically, the version of the database engine that they were running had a known vulnerability and they had to upgrade to a newer version.


During the upgrade, one of their larger databases did something unexpected. While converting data from the old format to the new one, it generated files well in excess of 2x the size of the old database. The team knew from watching the other databases that these files would be cleaned up after the upgrade, but there was no indication prior to the upgrade that this large total storage size would be required. These files used up all of the remaining space on their volume. The upgrade stalled, leaving the database in an indeterminate state, prompting the team to free up additional space to continue.


In order to free up space, the team inspected the other databases running on that volume. They identified the one that had unusually low concurrent connections. It was the best candidate that they could identify for deletion, to free up additional space. They consulted with each other and determined that the database might be unused –a relic of some prior architecture– but due to recent staff cuts, no one had institutional knowledge to know exactly what that database was used for, if anything.


In order to protect the large database that they knew was important, they all agreed to free up the seemingly unused database to allow the upgrade to continue. So they did, and the upgrade proceeded, but the next time the control plane tried to update its metrics, it could not do so because it relied on the deleted database to hold that information, which was only done on 30 minute cycles, which is why the database was usually idling. Alarms went off, and the rest of the incident proceeded as above.


Notice how different this narrative is from the first one in the report. The person who deleted the database was labeled incompetent in the first narrative; now they are making a reasonable judgment call in agreement with their peers, navigating out of a situation where there are no good options.


> The incident is in the past, so the facts didn’t change. It’s the same incident. But when we change the way we approach the story, with curiosity instead of judgment, we get a completely different story.


I’d call this an incident *investigation* . We had conversations and followed leads until we understood something about why the decisions that people made at the time, under pressure, were reasonable decisions to make.


### Could AI help with the investigation? Not likely.


Circa 2026, it is unlikely that humans would be comfortable enough speaking with AI agents to be honest and vulnerable about a charged work incident. It’s even less likely that an AI agent would have the situational context to know how to follow up with the right questions. *LLMs cannot empathize* . Also note that while the order of events and other stuff that AI can help with in a report is nice info to have, it doesn’t carry much relevance in the investigation narrative.


### Is this investigation useful? Definitely.


Not only does it exonerate the person who deleted the database, it destroys any perceived value in the retrospective RCA/COE. Deleting the database was not a root cause. Want to identify some contributing factors? How about these:


- Institutional knowledge is lost when the team was down-sized
- Security patches encourage risky operations in production
- Upgrade processes have ambiguous resource utilization
- Upgrade interruptions have ambiguous side effects


The prior action items also get thrown out the window. Guardrails would not have prevented the incident; if anything, they would have delayed the restoration of the large database, since the team would have had to find a way around those guardrails to do what they had consensus to do. How about these for some outcome recommendations instead of action items:


- Have management consider and justify the threat to reliability (loss of institutional knowledge) when pursuing efficiency (staff reductions on the team).
- Have Security sit through upgrades with a few operations teams, so they have more context about potential threats to availability.
- Redesign the tools or the system to provide better context to operators concerning the upgrade process and how it can go sideways


## So if AI writes the retrospective, does anyone learn?


Let’s return to the main question, and ask if it is the right question. What is the point of the retrospective? If the point is to check a box, then AI can be a huge benefit. And there are many valid business cases, like regulation and compliance, for checking a box. If the purpose is to learn, then[AI can provide some framework](https://www.usenix.org/conference/srecon26emea/presentation/allspaw) to the discussion. It can provide plot points, and identify main characters. But it can’t reach behind those details and uncover motives, anxiety, experience, and conflicting concerns. Each business needs to decide how important those things are.


Not every incident needs an investigation. They take time, both to conduct an investigation and to digest as a consumer of the final report or artifact. Our point is that the business should know what they get out of their current approach, know what they *can* get out of certain approaches, and choose what to do post-incident with eyes wide open. Tools like Rootly AI SRE can remove a lot of toil, freeing humans up to do the more important work, like talking to other humans.


> Perhaps the best advice we can give is to treat LLM-based tools not as artificial intelligence, but as augmented intelligence.


Rootly provides enough AI enablement to leverage agents where it makes sense to do so, for your business, for the types of incidents you care about.[Seventy percent of alerts at Rootly close without paging a human](https://rootly.com/great-incident-management) . That’s less toil for people, less interruption, more time to spend on more important things. *That* is a great benefit of AI.
